summaryTr: Gezgin satıcı Gregor Samsa bir sabah uyandığında korkunç bir yaratığa dönüştüğünü fark eder. Kafka'nın ünlü öyküsünün, ailesinin bu açıklanamayan olay karşısında nasıl değiştiğini anlatan kısaltılmış İngilizce uyarlaması.
paragraphs: ## I. The Morning

When Gregor Samsa woke one morning from uneasy dreams, he found that he had been changed, there in his bed, into some kind of monstrous vermin. He was lying on his back, which had become as hard as armour, and when he raised his head a little he could see his domed brown belly, divided by stiff curved ridges, with the blanket barely clinging to the top of it. His many legs, pitifully thin compared with the rest of him, flickered helplessly before his eyes.

“What has happened to me?” he thought. It was not a dream. His room, a proper human room, if a little too small, lay quietly between its four familiar walls. Above the table, where his samples of cloth were spread out – Samsa was a travelling salesman – hung a picture he had recently cut out of a magazine and put in a pretty gilt frame: a lady in a fur hat and fur stole, sitting upright and holding out a heavy fur muff into which her whole forearm had disappeared.

Rain was tapping on the window sill. Why not sleep a little longer and forget all this nonsense? But however hard he threw himself onto his right side, he rocked back again. “Oh God,” he thought, “what an exhausting job I’ve chosen! On the road day in, day out, worrying about train connections, eating bad meals at odd hours, meeting people who never become friends.” If it were not for his parents, he would have given notice long ago. But once he had saved enough to pay off their old debt to his boss – five or six more years, perhaps – he would make the great break. For now, though, he had to get up. His train left at five.

He glanced at the alarm clock ticking on the chest of drawers. It was half past six, and the hands were moving calmly on. Had he slept through the alarm? The next train went at seven, and the firm’s errand boy had certainly reported him already. Should he say he was ill? In five years he had never once been ill, and the insurance doctor believed that the whole world consisted of perfectly healthy people who simply disliked work. Besides, apart from a certain sleepiness, Gregor felt quite well. He was even unusually hungry.

There was a cautious knock at the door by the head of his bed. “Gregor,” called his mother, “it’s a quarter to seven. Weren’t you going to catch your train?” Gregor was shocked when he heard his reply. It was still his own voice, but mixed into it, as if from somewhere below, was a painful squeaking that left the words clear only for an instant and then blurred them. “Yes, yes, thank you, Mother, I’m getting up,” was all he said, and the wooden door seemed to hide the change. But now the whole family knew he was still at home. His father knocked at one side door, weakly but with his fist; at the other his sister asked softly, “Gregor? Aren’t you well? Do you need anything?” “I’m nearly ready,” he answered both of them, pronouncing every word with great care. His sister whispered, “Gregor, open the door, I beg you.” He had no intention of opening it. He was glad of the habit, picked up on his travels, of locking his doors at night, even at home.
## The Chief Clerk

Gregor did not doubt that the strange voice was simply the first sign of a heavy cold, the usual illness of salesmen. Throwing off the blanket was easy, but after that everything became difficult. He would have needed arms and hands to lift himself; instead he had only these little legs, which never stopped moving and which he could not control. In the end he began to rock his whole body out of bed.

He was already half out when the doorbell rang, and from the visitor’s first word of greeting he knew who it was: the chief clerk himself. More out of agitation than real decision, he swung himself out with all his strength and landed with a dull thump.

“Something fell in there,” said the chief clerk in the room on the left. “Gregor,” said his father, “the chief clerk wants to know why you didn’t take the early train. Please open the door.” “He isn’t well, sir, believe me,” his mother added. “The boy thinks of nothing but his work. His only amusement is fretwork – he carved a little picture frame, you’ll be amazed how pretty it is.” “So may the chief clerk come in now?” asked his impatient father. “No,” said Gregor. In the room on the left there was an awkward silence; in the room on the right his sister began to sob.

Then the chief clerk raised his voice. “Mr Samsa, what is going on? You barricade yourself in your room, worry your parents and neglect your duties in a quite unheard-of way. This morning the boss suggested an explanation for your absence – it concerned the payments recently entrusted to you – and I almost gave my word of honour that it could not be true. But your position is by no means secure. We recognise that this is not the season for exceptional business; but a season for doing no business at all does not exist, Mr Samsa. It must not exist.”

“But sir,” cried Gregor, beside himself, “I’ll open the door at once! A slight dizzy spell kept me in bed, but I’m quite well again now. Please spare my parents! I’ll take the eight o’clock train. Give my respects to the boss!” While he poured this out, he pushed himself across to the chest of drawers and, after slipping several times, stood upright against it.

“Did you understand a single word of that?” the chief clerk asked the parents. “For God’s sake,” cried his mother, “he may be seriously ill! Grete, run for the doctor!” “That was the voice of an animal,” said the chief clerk, strikingly quiet. “Anna!” the father shouted. “Fetch a locksmith at once!” The two girls ran out with rustling skirts and left the front door open behind them, as people do in homes where a great misfortune has happened.

Gregor, however, felt calmer. They no longer understood his words, but at least they believed something was wrong and were ready to help. He felt drawn back into the human circle. He pushed a chair to the door, held himself upright against it – the pads of his feet were a little sticky – and set about turning the key with his mouth. He seemed to have no real teeth, but his jaws were strong, though a brown liquid ran from his mouth and dripped onto the floor. “Listen,” said the chief clerk next door, “he’s turning the key.” Gregor bit into it with all his strength until the lock sprang back with a clear click. “So I didn’t need the locksmith after all,” he thought with relief.
## Through the Door

Because of the way he had to open it, the door was already wide open before Gregor himself could be seen. He was still edging carefully round it when he heard the chief clerk let out a loud “Oh!”, like a rush of wind. The man pressed his hand to his open mouth and slowly backed away, as if pushed by an invisible force. His mother, her hair still loose from the night, took two steps towards Gregor and sank to the floor among her spreading skirts, her face hidden. His father clenched his fist with a hostile expression, as if to knock Gregor back into his room, then covered his eyes with his hands and wept until his broad chest shook.

“Well,” said Gregor, well aware that he was the only one who had kept calm, “I’ll get dressed, pack my samples and leave at once. You see, sir, I’m not stubborn, and I like my work. I’m in a tight spot, but I’ll work my way out of it. Please take my side at the office!” But at his first words the chief clerk had turned away and was backing towards the hall without taking his eyes off Gregor. Once there, he stretched his hand towards the stairs as if some heavenly rescue were waiting for him.

Gregor knew he must not let the man go in this mood, or his job was lost. He let go of the door, pushed himself through, and fell with a little cry onto his many legs. At once, for the first time that morning, he felt a kind of physical well-being: his legs had firm ground beneath them and obeyed him perfectly. He believed that the end of all his suffering was near.

At that moment his mother sprang up, arms outstretched. “Help, for God’s sake, help!” she screamed, ran backwards against the breakfast table and sat down on it, not noticing that coffee was pouring from the overturned pot onto the carpet. “Mother, Mother,” said Gregor softly, and at the sight of the flowing coffee he could not stop his jaws from snapping at the air. His mother screamed again and fled into his father’s arms.

But the chief clerk was already on the stairs. Gregor took a run after him; the man leapt down several steps at once and vanished, a last “Ugh!” echoing through the stairwell. This flight seemed to confuse the father completely. He seized the walking stick the visitor had left on a chair, took a large newspaper in his other hand, and, stamping his feet and hissing like a savage, began to drive Gregor back into his room. No pleading helped; none was understood. When at last Gregor managed to turn round, his body was too wide for the half-open door, and it did not occur to his father to open the other half. Gregor forced himself into the gap and stuck there, one side scraped raw, ugly stains left on the white door – until his father gave him a powerful push from behind that was truly a release, and he flew, bleeding heavily, far into his room. The door was slammed shut with the stick. Then, at last, it was quiet.
## II. A Sister’s Care

It was dusk before Gregor woke. One of his legs had been badly hurt and dragged behind him, and his left side felt like one long, tight scar. By the door he found a bowl of sweet milk with pieces of white bread floating in it. Milk had always been his favourite drink, and his sister had surely put it there for that reason, but now he could not bear it and turned away almost in disgust. That night the high, empty room frightened him, and with a slight feeling of shame he hurried under the sofa, where he felt immediately comfortable. He decided that for the present he must keep quiet and, through patience and the greatest consideration, make his condition as bearable as possible for his family.

Early next morning his sister looked in. When she saw him under the sofa, she slammed the door in fright; then, as if she regretted it, she came in on tiptoe, as one might enter the room of a stranger. She noticed the untouched milk and, out of pure kindness, brought him a whole selection on an old newspaper to test his taste: half-rotten vegetables, bones in a sauce that had set, raisins and almonds, a cheese Gregor had called inedible two days before, and some bread. Then she left quickly, knowing he would not eat in front of her. With eyes watering with satisfaction, he devoured the cheese, the vegetables and the sauce. The fresh food he could not even stand the smell of.

From then on she fed him twice a day. Since nobody understood him, it never occurred to anyone that he could understand them. “He liked it today,” she would say; or, more and more often, almost sadly, “Everything’s been left again.” By pressing himself to the doors, he learned other things. The maid had begged on her knees to be dismissed. And his father, whose business had collapsed five years earlier, had kept back a small sum from those days; part of Gregor’s monthly earnings had been saved as well. Gregor nodded eagerly behind his door, pleased by this unexpected caution. Of course, the money might have paid off more of the debt and freed him from his job sooner; but no doubt it was better the way his father had arranged it.

After that collapse he had thrown himself into work and laid his earnings on the table before his astonished family. Those had been wonderful times, but the family had simply got used to it, and the old warmth had never come back. Only his sister had stayed close to him. She loved music and played the violin movingly, and it was his secret plan to send her to the conservatory next year, whatever it cost. He had meant to announce it on Christmas Eve.

But the savings would last a year, two at most. His father was old and had grown fat; his mother had asthma; his sister was only seventeen. Whenever the talk turned to earning money, Gregor threw himself onto the cool leather sofa, burning with shame and grief. At night he pushed a chair to the window and leaned against the glass, though day by day he saw less, until the street outside seemed a wasteland where grey sky and grey earth merged into one.

His sister still could not bear the sight of him. Each time she came in, she ran straight to the window and tore it open as if she were suffocating. So one day – it took him four hours – Gregor carried a sheet on his back to the sofa and arranged it so that he was completely hidden. She left it there, and once, when he lifted a corner with his head, he thought he caught a grateful look.
## The Empty Room

To pass the time, Gregor began crawling across the walls and ceiling. He loved hanging up there; he could breathe more freely, and in his almost happy absent-mindedness he sometimes let go and dropped to the floor without hurting himself. His sister noticed the sticky traces he left and decided to give him more room by taking out the furniture, above all the chest of drawers and the desk. She could not do it alone, so one day, while their father was out, she fetched their mother.

Gregor pulled the sheet low and listened as the two weak women shifted the heavy chest. After a quarter of an hour his mother whispered, “Doesn’t it look as if, by taking away his furniture, we’re showing him that we’ve given up all hope? I think we should leave the room exactly as it was, so that when Gregor comes back to us, he finds everything unchanged and can forget this time more easily.”

Hearing her voice, Gregor realised that two months in which nobody had spoken directly to him must have confused his mind. Did he really want his warm room, furnished with family pieces, turned into a cave where he could crawl in every direction while quickly forgetting his human past? He was close to forgetting already. Nothing should be removed. Everything had to stay.

But Grete had grown used to acting as the expert on Gregor’s affairs, and her mother’s advice only made her insist on clearing out everything except the sofa. Perhaps, too, some romantic urge tempted her to make his situation even more frightening, so that she could do even more for him. For into a room where Gregor ruled the bare walls alone, nobody but Grete would ever dare to enter.

So the chest went, with his fretsaw and tools inside, and they began loosening the desk at which he had done his homework since he was a little boy. He could bear it no longer. He broke out from under the sofa, changed direction four times, not knowing what to save first, and then saw, on the otherwise bare wall, the lady dressed in fur. He crawled up and pressed himself against the glass, which felt pleasant against his hot belly. This picture, at least, nobody would take away.

When the women returned, Grete’s eyes met his on the wall. Trembling, she tried to lead her mother back out of the room, but her mother stepped aside, saw the huge brown stain on the flowered wallpaper, and, before she understood that it was Gregor, cried out, “Oh God, oh God!” and fell across the sofa with her arms spread wide. “You, Gregor!” cried his sister, raising her fist. They were the first words she had spoken directly to him since his transformation. She ran next door for smelling salts. Gregor tore himself from the glass and followed, as if he could advise her as in the old days; she turned, saw him and dropped a bottle, and a splinter cut his face. Grete grabbed what bottles she could and ran back to her mother, kicking the door shut. Cut off and tormented by self-reproach, Gregor crawled over everything – walls, furniture, ceiling – until the whole room seemed to spin, and he fell onto the middle of the big table.
## The Apples

The doorbell rang. It was his father. “Mother fainted, but she’s better now,” said Grete. “Gregor has broken out.” “I knew it,” said his father. “I always told you, but you women never listen.” Gregor saw that his father had imagined some act of violence, and he hurried to the door of his room to show that he wanted only to go back in.

“Ah!” cried his father as he entered, in a tone at once furious and glad. Gregor looked up at him. Was this really his father – the man who used to lie wearily in bed when Gregor left on his trips, who greeted him in the evenings in his dressing gown, who on their rare Sunday walks shuffled along on his stick? Now he stood up straight in a tight blue uniform with gold buttons, like those worn by bank messengers; his white hair was combed into a shining parting. He threw his cap across the room onto the sofa and came towards Gregor with a grim face, lifting his feet unusually high. Gregor was amazed at the enormous size of his boot soles.

Gregor ran ahead of him, stopping when his father stopped and hurrying on when he moved. They circled the room several times like this, so slowly that it hardly looked like a chase. But Gregor was already short of breath. Then something flew past him and rolled across the floor. It was an apple; a second followed at once. His father had filled his pockets from the fruit bowl on the sideboard and was throwing them one after another. The little red apples rolled about as if electrified. One grazed Gregor’s back and slid off harmlessly; but the next one actually drove itself into his back. He tried to drag himself on, as if the incredible pain might stay behind, but he felt nailed to the spot. With his last glance he saw his mother rush out of his room in her petticoat, her loosened skirts slipping to the floor one after another, throw herself upon his father, embrace him and, with her hands clasped behind his head, beg him to spare Gregor’s life.
## III. Evenings with the Door Open

The apple stayed lodged in Gregor’s flesh as a visible souvenir, since nobody dared to remove it, and he suffered from the wound for more than a month. It seemed to remind even his father that Gregor, despite his repulsive shape, was a member of the family, and that family duty required them to swallow their disgust and be patient, nothing but patient. Crossing his room now took Gregor long minutes, like an old invalid, and climbing was out of the question. But in exchange, every evening the living room door was left open, so that he could lie in the dark and watch the whole family at the lit table.

These were no longer the lively evenings he had longed for in small hotel rooms. His father, who refused to take off his uniform even at home, fell asleep in his chair after supper; his mother sewed fine linen for a fashion shop; his sister, now a shop assistant, studied shorthand and French. At ten it took the two women a quarter of an hour to coax the father to bed. “What a life,” he would sigh. “So this is the peace of my old age.”

Who in this overworked family had time for Gregor? The maid was dismissed; a huge, bony charwoman with white hair came morning and evening for the heaviest work. Family jewellery was sold. They said they could not leave the flat, now too big for them, because of Gregor – though he could easily have been carried in a box with a few air holes. What really held them back was hopelessness, and the feeling that they had been struck by a misfortune like no one else they knew.

His sister no longer wondered what might please him. Before work she pushed any food at all into his room with her foot, and in the evening she swept it out again, usually untouched. Dirt streaked the walls; balls of dust lay in the corners. Yet when their mother once scrubbed the room, Grete, deeply offended, burst into tears, the father shouted at both women, and Gregor hissed with rage that nobody thought to close the door.

The charwoman was not afraid of him at all. She liked to open his door and call in, with words she probably thought friendly, “Come over here, you old dung beetle!” Once, in the early morning, while a heavy rain – perhaps already a sign of spring – beat against the windows, he turned towards her as if to attack, slowly and feebly. She simply raised a chair high above her head, her mouth wide open. “So that’s as far as you go?” she asked when he turned away, and calmly put the chair back in the corner.
## The Violin

Gregor now ate almost nothing. The family had let one of their rooms to three lodgers, serious gentlemen with full beards who insisted on order everywhere, especially in the kitchen. Everything they did not need – old furniture, the ash bin, the rubbish bin – was thrown into Gregor’s room, and he crawled through the junk, later with growing pleasure, though afterwards he lay for hours, tired to death and sad.

One evening the charwoman left the living room door slightly open. The lodgers sat down at the head of the table, where Gregor and his parents used to sit, and the mother and sister brought in steaming dishes of meat and potatoes. The family itself ate in the kitchen. Gregor, listening, could always hear the lodgers’ chewing teeth, as if to show him that one needed teeth to eat. “I am hungry,” he said to himself sadly, “but not for these things. How these lodgers feed themselves, while I am dying!”

That same evening the violin sounded from the kitchen. The lodgers asked whether the young lady would not like to play in the living room instead, where it was more comfortable. “Oh, please,” said the father, as if he were the violinist himself. The parents, who had never let rooms before, did not even dare to sit on their own chairs.

His sister began to play. Drawn by the music, Gregor ventured forward until his head was in the living room. Covered in dust, with threads and scraps of food clinging to his back, he was not ashamed to advance across the spotless floor. Nobody noticed him. The lodgers soon withdrew to the window, blowing cigar smoke towards the ceiling; they were obviously disappointed and tolerated the music only out of politeness. And yet his sister played so beautifully. Her head was tilted, her eyes following the notes, searching and sad. Was he an animal, when music moved him so? He felt as if a way were opening before him to the unknown nourishment he longed for. He would reach her, tug at her skirt and let her know that she should bring her violin into his room, for nobody here valued her playing as he did. He would never let her out again; his frightful shape would be useful for the first time. He would tell her that he had meant to send her to the conservatory – and she would burst into tears of emotion, and he would raise himself to her shoulder and kiss her neck.

“Mr Samsa!” called the middle gentleman, pointing at Gregor. The violin stopped. The father rushed to push the lodgers back into their room, and now they did grow angry. In the doorway the middle gentleman stamped his foot. “I hereby declare,” he said, “that in view of the disgusting conditions in this flat and family” – here he spat on the floor – “I give notice at once. Of course I shall not pay a penny for the days I have lived here, and I shall consider whether to bring a claim against you.” “We also give notice at once,” said his two friends, and the door slammed.
## It Has to Go

The father staggered to his chair. Gregor lay where he had been caught, too weak and too disappointed to move. Not even the violin startled him when it slipped from his mother’s trembling fingers and fell with a ringing sound.

“My dear parents,” said his sister, striking the table with her hand, “things can’t go on like this. I won’t say my brother’s name in front of this monster, so I’ll only say: we must try to get rid of it. We’ve done everything humanly possible to look after it and put up with it. Nobody can blame us in the least.”

“She’s absolutely right,” said the father to himself. The mother began to cough dully into her hand. “It will be the death of you both,” Grete went on, weeping. “When we all have to work as hard as we do, we can’t bear this endless torment at home as well. I can’t bear it any more.”
“But child,” said the father, “what are we to do? If he understood us, perhaps we could come to some arrangement with him. But as it is –”

“It has to go,” cried his sister. “That’s the only way, Father. You just have to get rid of the idea that it’s Gregor. Our real misfortune is that we’ve believed it for so long. If it were Gregor, he would have realised long ago that people can’t live with such an animal, and he would have gone away of his own accord. Then we wouldn’t have a brother, but we could go on living and honour his memory. Instead it persecutes us, drives away the lodgers, and obviously wants the whole flat for itself.”

Gregor had not the slightest wish to frighten anyone, least of all his sister. He had only begun, slowly and with great effort, to turn round and crawl back to his room. They all watched him in sad silence. Nobody hurried him. He was astonished at the great distance to his door. As he reached it, he turned his head – not completely, for his neck was growing stiff – and saw that nothing behind him had changed, except that his sister had stood up. His last glance fell on his mother, who was now fast asleep.
He was hardly inside when the door was pushed shut, bolted and locked. “At last!” his sister called to her parents as she turned the key.

“And now?” Gregor asked himself, looking around in the dark. He soon discovered that he could no longer move at all. This did not surprise him. He had pains all over, but they seemed to be growing fainter. He could hardly feel the rotten apple in his back or the inflamed area around it, now covered in soft dust. He thought back on his family with tenderness and love. His opinion that he must disappear was, if possible, even firmer than his sister’s. He remained in this state of empty and peaceful reflection until the tower clock struck three in the morning. He still saw the first light growing outside the window. Then, without his willing it, his head sank down completely, and from his nostrils his last breath flowed out faintly.
## Spring

Early in the morning the charwoman arrived, slamming every door as usual. Thinking Gregor was sulking, she poked him with her long broom, and only when he slid away without resistance did she understand. She whistled to herself, tore open the bedroom door and called loudly into the darkness: “Come and have a look, it’s croaked; there it lies, dead as a doornail!”

Mr and Mrs Samsa hurried into Gregor’s room, and Grete, fully dressed and pale as if she had not slept, came from the living room. “Dead?” said Mrs Samsa. “I should say so,” said the charwoman, and pushed the body a good way to one side with her broom. Mrs Samsa made a movement as if to stop her, but did not. “Well,” said Mr Samsa, “now we can thank God.” He crossed himself, and the three women followed his example. “Look how thin he was,” said Grete. “He hadn’t eaten anything for so long.” Indeed, Gregor’s body was completely flat and dry. The charwoman opened the window wide. There was already a certain mildness in the air; it was, after all, the end of March.

When the lodgers came out asking for their breakfast, Mr Samsa appeared in his uniform, his wife on one arm and his daughter on the other. “Leave my flat at once!” he said. “What do you mean?” asked the middle gentleman with a sugary smile. “I mean exactly what I say.” The lodger looked at the floor for a moment, as if his thoughts were arranging themselves in a new order. “Then we’ll go,” he said, and the three men took their hats and sticks, bowed silently and left.

The family decided to spend the day resting and going for a walk; they had earned the break, and they needed it. So they sat down and wrote three letters of excuse to their employers. The charwoman came in, smiling, the little ostrich feather on her hat swaying. “You don’t need to worry about how to get rid of that thing next door,” she said. “It’s all been taken care of.” Mr Samsa stopped her with an outstretched hand before she could describe it, and she left, offended, slamming the door. “She’ll be dismissed this evening,” said Mr Samsa. Then he called to his wife and daughter, who were standing at the window with their arms around each other: “Come here, then. Let the old things go at last. And show a little consideration for me.” They hurried to him, caressed him and quickly finished their letters.

Then all three of them left the flat together, which they had not done for months, and took the tram out into the open country beyond the city. The carriage, in which they were the only passengers, was full of warm sunshine. They talked about the future and found that, on closer inspection, their prospects were not bad at all, for all three jobs were good and especially promising. Above all, they would move to a smaller, cheaper and more practical flat than the one Gregor had chosen. Mr and Mrs Samsa, watching their daughter grow livelier all the time, noticed almost at the same moment how, in spite of all the hardship that had made her cheeks pale, she had blossomed into a pretty young woman. Growing quieter, and understanding each other almost without words, they thought that it would soon be time to find her a good husband. And it seemed to them like a confirmation of their new dreams and good intentions when, at the end of the journey, their daughter was the first to get up and stretch her young body.
